doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

title: Playing with Monk, his time and five-tuplets
summary: Smith had listened to and transcribed Monk since 16. He says Monk plays perfect five-tuplets mixed with triplets, never dragging.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: You were speaking about comping and piano players. I wonder if working with Thelonious and his distinctive style of playing affected the way you played? Did you feel you needed to play slightly different with him?

No. No I was playing for Thelonious and I had been listening to Thelonious since I was 16 and avidly, and very familiar with his music. And I had transcribed some of his more difficult tunes and on the west coast there weren’t that many people that were into Thelonious at all. But I just really loved his compositions and he had a peculiar way, and I was, as years have gone on and I’ve broadened my scope of understanding of time — what they used to say well you know he plays these, he kind of plays these — he’s dragging these triplets you know in a certain way. And they go that’s Thelonious, you know, he kind of drags the triplets and this thing. But you know when I studied, oh I guess it was 25 years ago I began studying five-tuplets, you know, and so I spent six months studying that and everything and becoming like an eighth note five-tuplet is a quarter note five-tuplets, half note five-tuplets, and to where it becomes — and the process for me has always been I’ll get a night, and for some reason I want to do this. So I spent this time trying to assimilate five-tuplets and trying to put it my playing and it wouldn’t go. You know. And so finally after six months I said okay that’s — and then two years later I’m listening to a playback of something I’m on, a recording, and I listened back and I’m playing perfect five-tuplets. And they don’t sound weird at all. And the music is full of them. You know like a lot of tunes are full of five-tuplets. And then when I heard, you know I don’t listen to Thelonious like sometimes maybe for five years you know I don’t listen to him. And then I heard a Thelonious thing and I realized, my God he’s playing perfect five-tuplets. Perfect five-tuplets. Only he’s able to mix in triplets and sixteens and five-tuplets. You know? And threw it all in, but it’s all in time. He’s never dragging. And he was so — anyway —
Was it apparent on the gig — did he show pleasure or otherwise with the way the band was sounding? Could you tell if he was pleased or not?
